basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: Name the wave type in which vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
back: Longitudinal.

base_cards.front: What does the amplitude of a wave measure?
back: The maximum displacement from the resting position.

base_cards.front: Give the approximate upper frequency limit of normal human hearing.
back: 20 kHz.

base_cards.front: Which electromagnetic group lies between visible light and X-rays?
back: Ultraviolet.

base_cards.front: What type of image can be formed on a screen?
back: Real.

base_cards.front: Name the line from which angles of incidence and reflection are measured.
back: The normal.

base_cards.front: Which seismic wave cannot travel through liquids?
back: S-wave.

base_cards.front: What happens to a wave’s frequency when it enters a different medium?
back: It stays the same.

base_cards.front: What is a perfect black body?
back: An object that absorbs all radiation incident on it.

base_cards.front: Compare particle vibrations in transverse and longitudinal waves.
back: Transverse vibrations are **perpendicular** to energy transfer.
Longitudinal vibrations are **parallel** to energy transfer.

base_cards.front: A cork bobs in a ripple tank but stays in approximately the same horizontal position. Explain what this shows.
back: The cork and nearby water move locally as the disturbance passes.
The wave transfers **energy without an overall transfer of the water** across the tank.

base_cards.front: A wave has frequency 25 Hz. Calculate its period.
A ripple has frequency 5.0 Hz and wavelength 0.060 m. Calculate its speed.
Why is a distance–displacement wave graph unsuitable for reading the period directly?
back: Its horizontal axis shows **distance**, so a full cycle gives wavelength.
Period needs a **time axis** or a separate timing measurement.

base_cards.front: A ray strikes a mirror at 35° to the normal. State its reflection angle and its angle to the mirror surface.
back: Reflection angle = **35°**.
Angle to the surface = 90° − 35° = **55°**.

base_cards.front: Explain why rough surfaces scatter reflected light even though the reflection law still applies.
back: Different small parts of the surface have **different normal directions**.
Each obeys i = r, but the reflected rays travel in **different directions**.

base_cards.front: Why can ultrasound be used to find a hidden boundary?
back: Some ultrasound is **reflected at a boundary between different materials**.
The returning echo’s time delay reveals the boundary’s **distance**, using the wave speed.

base_cards.front: Explain why S-wave observations support a liquid outer core.
back: S-waves **cannot travel through liquids**.
Their failure to pass through the outer core supports the conclusion that it is **liquid**.

base_cards.front: Why are X-rays suitable for an image of a broken bone?
back: Bone **absorbs more X-rays** than surrounding soft tissue.
Different amounts reaching the detector produce **contrast**, showing the bone and fracture.

base_cards.front: Explain why a red shirt appears dark under only blue light.
back: It mostly **absorbs blue** and reflects red.
There is little red in the illumination, so **little light reaches the eye from the shirt**.

base_cards.front: A lens forms a 30 mm image of a 12 mm object. Calculate magnification and state whether it has a unit.
back: Magnification = 30/12 = **2.5**, with **no unit**.

base_cards.front: Explain why an object cools by radiation when it emits 80 W and absorbs 50 W.
back: It loses energy at a **net rate of 30 W**.
More radiation is emitted than absorbed, so its **temperature falls**, assuming no other transfers balance the loss.

base_cards.front: Why must the distance between an infrared detector and each Leslie-cube face be the same?
back: Detector reading changes with distance.
Keeping distance constant helps ensure differences are caused by **surface finish**, rather than measurement position.

base_cards.front: Two students report reflection angles of 29.1° and 29.2° using a protractor marked every 1°. Explain the problem.
back: The instrument’s **resolution is 1°**.
It does not resolve a **0.1° difference**, so those readings imply unjustified precision.

base_cards.front: How can radio waves be generated and then detected in electrical circuits?
back: **Oscillating electrical currents** generate radio waves.
Absorbed radio waves can induce an **alternating current at the same frequency** in a receiving circuit.

base_cards.front: Sound of frequency 400 Hz travels at 340 m/s in air and 1,500 m/s in water. Calculate its wavelength in both media and explain the frequency.
back: Frequency remains **400 Hz** because it is set by the source.

base_cards.front: A microwave travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and has wavelength 12.0 cm. Calculate its frequency in standard form.
An echo returns 0.060 s after a pulse is sent through water. Sound travels at 1,480 m/s. Calculate the distance to the reflector.
back: Total travelled distance = vt = 1,480 × 0.060 = **88.8 m**.
This is the **out-and-back** journey.
Distance to reflector = 88.8/2 = **44.4 m**.

base_cards.front: Explain why a light ray entering glass obliquely bends towards the normal.
back: Parts of a wavefront reach the glass at **different times**.
Light travels **more slowly in glass**, so one part slows before another.
The wavefront turns, changing the ray’s direction **towards the normal**.

base_cards.front: A convex lens is used as a magnifying glass. Where is the object, and what are three properties of its image?
back: Object is **closer to the lens than its focal length**.
Image is **virtual and upright**.
It is **magnified**, on the same side as the object.

base_cards.front: Explain one benefit and two precautions when using X-rays for medical imaging.
back: They can reveal internal structures such as **bone fractures** without surgery.
Use the **lowest dose that gives useful information**, limiting exposure time and unnecessary repeats.
Use appropriate **shielding** for staff and unaffected areas where suitable, because ionising radiation can damage cells.

base_cards.front: Six consecutive crest lines span 0.15 m in a ripple tank. Frequency is 12 Hz. Calculate wavelength and speed.
back: Six crest lines contain **five wavelengths**.

base_cards.front: A string has four stationary loops across 1.20 m and vibrates at 50 Hz. Calculate the travelling wave’s wavelength and speed.
back: Each loop spans **half a wavelength**.

base_cards.front: White light passes through an ideal red filter and then an ideal blue filter. Explain why almost no light emerges.
back: The first filter **transmits red light** and absorbs other visible wavelengths.
The second mainly **transmits blue** and absorbs red.
Little of the light leaving the first filter can pass the second; filters **do not create new colours**.

base_cards.front: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound using two microphones.
back: Measure the **separation** of microphones connected to a data logger or oscilloscope.
Make a sharp sound in line with them and identify the **same pulse** in both recordings.
Measure arrival-time difference and calculate **v = separation/time delay**.
Repeat and average. Use enough separation for a measurable delay; electronic timing avoids human reaction-time error.

base_cards.front: Explain how a warming object’s emitted radiation changes and what radiation balance means.
back: It emits **more energy per second** as temperature rises.
Its spectrum shifts towards **shorter wavelengths**.
At constant temperature, absorbed and emitted power balance if radiation is the only energy transfer.
If absorbed power exceeds emitted power, its **temperature rises** until the balance changes.

base_cards.front: An IR experiment compares a black and a shiny surface. The black surface starts hotter and is closer to the detector. Explain why the result does not isolate the effect of surface finish and how to improve it.
back: **Hotter surfaces emit more**, so starting-temperature differences affect the readings.
**Distance** also affects the detector’s reading.
Use faces at the **same temperature**, for example on one hot Leslie cube.
Keep **detector distance and angle fixed**, repeat, and compare readings.

additions.front: What happens to wavelength if source frequency doubles while wave speed stays fixed?
back: Wavelength halves.

additions.front: At 340 m/s, what wavelength corresponds to 170 Hz?
What period follows from four complete cycles in 8.0 ms?
What frequency corresponds to a 0.0020 s period?
Why must both construction rays start from the same object point?
back: Their intersection locates the image of that particular point.

additions.front: Do dashed virtual-image extensions show actual light travelling backwards?
back: No. They show where diverging rays appear to originate.

additions.front: Why cannot a screen capture a concave lens’s virtual image of a real object?
back: Actual emerging rays do not converge at the apparent image location.

additions.front: Can a convex lens produce a virtual image?
back: Yes, when the object is closer to it than its focal length.

additions.front: Why can a yellow object appear red in red illumination?
back: It can reflect the available red component; green light is not present.

additions.front: Why does a cyan filter transmit little red-only light?
back: It mainly transmits green and blue and absorbs most red; it cannot create missing colours.

additions.front: What is net radiative gain for 100 W absorbed and 80 W emitted?
back: 20 W, or 20 J each second.

additions.front: Does constant temperature imply zero infrared emission?
back: No. Emission can balance absorption at a non-zero rate.

additions.front: Why use the wave speed for the material in an ultrasound question?
back: Sound speed depends on the medium; an air value is not suitable for body tissue or water.

additions.front: What must be halved when converting a returning echo time into boundary distance?
back: The total out-and-back travel distance, giving d = vt/2.
